Tesla (NasdaqGS:TSLA) is reported to be in advanced merger talks with SpaceX, exploring a potential combination of the two Musk-led groups.

The company is widely rolling out its Full Self Driving 14.3 software update alongside specialized insurance for its autonomous Cybercab service.

Regulators and existing shareholders of both Tesla and SpaceX are expected to review detailed merger terms if negotiations progress to a formal proposal.

How could a Tesla and SpaceX merger reshape the business mix?

The proposed US$3.5t plus all stock combination would join Tesla's EV, robotics and energy units with SpaceX's launch, satellite and Starlink operations. That concentrates Elon Musk's projects into a single group built around AI, chip design and physical infrastructure, while raising questions about how ownership is split between existing Tesla and SpaceX investors.

Does this change the Tesla Narrative on autonomy and AI spend?

The current Narrative already leans on FSD subscriptions, Cybercab robotaxis and heavy capex in AI chips and Optimus, with analysts modeling earnings growth built on those platforms. A merger that pools AI infrastructure and Terafab semiconductor plans with SpaceX's data and Starlink network would support the existing catalyst that Tesla's large investment phase is aimed at scaled, software heavy services rather than just selling cars.

The key checkpoint is Cybercab deployment and insurance take up as orders open and deliveries are projected to start in December 2026. Tesla Sinks 8%, SpaceX Down 7%, Rivian Down 8% as AI Sell-Off Swamps HSBC Upgrade ©U.S. Air Force photo and Nikada from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Tesla fell 8% today as a sell-off in AI and growth stocks outweighed HSBC's upgrade to Hold with a $359 target.

HSBC values Tesla at $507 a share in a SpaceX deal and $212 on its own, so much of the price rests on a deal with no terms yet.

SpaceX fell on worries about its AI-chip debt, and Rivian, Applied Digital and IREN dropped in the wider sell-off.

Hold looks right until the companies release terms, which reports say could come as soon as December.

Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) fell 8% today, and a Wall Street upgrade couldn't stop it.

HSBC raised Tesla to Hold from Reduce before the open. But AI and growth stocks kept falling a day after the biggest IPO on record. SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ), which is exploring a merger with Tesla, fell 8% on worries about its AI-chip debt.

Rivian (RIVN:NASDAQ) has no part in the merger talks and still lost 8%. AI-infrastructure stocks fell the most: Applied Digital (APLD:NASDAQ) dropped 18% and IREN (IREN:NASDAQ) fell 17%, and neither had news of its own.

HSBC put a price on the merger

HSBC analyst Michael Tyndall raised his price target to $359 from $157. He values Tesla at $507 a share if SpaceX acquires it, assuming a 33% premium to the stock's 30-day average price, and at $212 on its own. That stand-alone value is only about 57% of Thursday's close. If HSBC is right, more than 40% of the stock price depends on SpaceX.

The stand-alone value is low because Tesla's earnings have been shrinking:

Tesla (TSLA): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

Normalized EPS fell to $1.66 in 2025 from $3.12 in 2023, and analysts don't expect it to beat the 2023 level until 2028.

Investors are also paying a much higher multiple for those earnings than the stock's own history would suggest:

Tesla (TSLA): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

Tesla closed Thursday at 175x forward earnings, against a five-year average of 109x.

TIKR tracks 44 analysts on Tesla. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Tesla, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Tesla's Analyst Ratings

Hold looks right to me

An offer paid in SpaceX stock would rise and fall with SpaceX's share price, and SpaceX fell today on its own borrowing. It sold $32 billion of bonds on Thursday to buy AI chips, at yields above 8%, Bloomberg reported. That AI build-out is exactly what investors are selling today.

Both companies have formed special committees of independent directors to explore a deal, but there are no terms yet.

The way I see it, a stock trading near HSBC's $359 target asks you to pay for a deal that doesn't exist yet, in shares that just fell on debt worries. Reports suggest an announcement could come as soon as December. A premium close to HSBC's 33% would support the $507 case. If talks collapse, HSBC's math points to $212.

title: Tesla (TSLA) Down 0.1% Since Last Earnings Report: Can It Rebound?
detail:
Tesla (TSLA) Down 0.1% Since Last Earnings Report: Can It Rebound?
Zacks Equity Research
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 8:30 AM MST 6 min read
TSLA
^GSPC
GM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A month has gone by since the last earnings report for Tesla (TSLA). Shares have lost about 0.1% in that time frame, outperforming the S&P 500.

But investors have to be wondering, will the recent negative trend continue leading up to its next earnings release, or is Tesla due for a breakout? Before we dive into how investors and analysts have reacted as of late, let's take a quick look at the latest earnings report in order to get a better handle on the important drivers.

Tesla Q3 Earnings Beat

Tesla reported third-quarter 2026 adjusted earnings of 48 cents per share, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of 45 cents by 6.67%. However, earnings declined 4% from 50 cents in the year-ago quarter, reflecting higher operating expenses.

Revenues totaled $28.05 billion, down marginally from $28.1 billion a year ago. Revenues surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $27.78 billion by 0.96%.

Growing Full Self-Driving (FSD) adoption and strength in services supported results.

Vehicle Deliveries Fall Despite Strong Demand

Tesla produced 464,391 vehicles during the quarter, up 4% year over year. Model 3/Y production increased 5% to 457,387 units, while production of other models declined 40% to 7,004 units.

Vehicle deliveries declined 2% year over year to 486,532 units. Model 3/Y deliveries slipped 1% to 478,237 units, while other model deliveries plunged 48% to 8,295 units. Global vehicle inventory was 11 days of supply compared with 10 days a year earlier.

Management highlighted record quarterly deliveries across several markets, including Canada, Australia, Japan and Taiwan. Tesla exited the quarter with its highest passenger vehicle order backlog in four years.

Deliveries were primarily constrained by production, with battery availability remaining a key bottleneck in increasing vehicle output.

Automotive Revenues Decline, Margins Improve

Automotive revenues declined 3% year over year to $20.56 billion. Automotive sales contributed $20.09 billion, while regulatory credit revenues dropped to $113 million from $417 million. Automotive leasing revenues totaled $353 million compared with $429 million a year ago.

Despite lower revenues, automotive gross margin improved to 18.5% from 17% in the year-ago period. Excluding regulatory credits, automotive gross margin expanded sequentially to 18.1% from 16.3%.

Management attributed the sequential improvement to a favorable regional delivery mix, particularly increased deliveries in Asia Pacific. However, lower vehicle average selling prices and reduced regulatory credit revenues remained headwinds.

Can Tesla (TSLA) Robotaxis Catch Waymo? JPMorgan Is Watching
Maham Fatima

Trade Tesla on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

We just published a list of the 10 Potential Multibagger Stocks to Research for Long-Term Growth and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) ranked 8th on this list.

Reuters reported on November 5 that the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24,315, its deepest one-day drop in 19 months, while the S&P 500 lost 4.36% and about $3 trillion in market value disappeared. The trigger was Democratic wins in Congress, including in states where opposition to new data centers has grown. That stoked fears that tougher regulation could slow the AI buildout that helped lift stocks to records this year. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged more than 12% on the day, according to the same report, and for anyone searching for stocks that could double over three to five years, a selloff of that size moves the conversation from momentum to staying power.

Can Tesla (TSLA) Robotaxis Catch Waymo? JPMorgan Is Watching
Why AI Took the Biggest Hit

Melissa Brown, a global head of investment decision research, told Reuters that investors appear to be recognizing that new lawmakers and governors want to slow AI infrastructure development. She added that the AI growth story has largely depended on building out the supporting infrastructure, so any slowdown raises real concerns. Those concerns fall hardest on companies whose growth is tied to data center spending. Our ranking of AI infrastructure stocks to hold for the long term covers that group in more detail.

The weakness carried into the following week. Reuters reported on November 16 that the Nasdaq tumbled 2.5% and the S&P 500 dropped nearly 2%, as fallout from the resignation of a leading chipmaker's chief executive soured enthusiasm for AI stocks. Rate worries added to the pressure. According to the Associated Press, minutes released on November 18 showed that nearly all Federal Reserve officials expect a 25-basis-point rate increase in December, and two floated a 50-basis-point move.

What Long-Term Investors Weigh

Not everyone read the November 5 selloff as the start of a longer slide. Jed Ellerbroek, a portfolio manager, told Reuters it felt like the capitulation phase for companies that benefit from data center spending. Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst, added that investors buying into a major AI public offering may sell existing tech holdings to pay for it. That concern showed up on November 19, when Reuters reported that the Nasdaq turned negative at midday as the AI developer's record-setting debut cast a cloud over AI-linked stocks. That leaves a market weighing policy risk, borrowing costs and AI demand all at once, and our list of undervalued growth stocks looks at the valuation side of that trade-off.

title: Elon Musk sends stark signal to Tesla stock investors
detail:
Elon Musk sends stark signal to Tesla stock investors
Hillary Remy, Celine Provini
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 8:17 AM MST 5 min read
TSLA
Trade Tesla on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Elon Musk is not done taking the driver out of the car.

Speaking at the DealBook Summit on Nov. 18, the Tesla CEO said the company plans an autonomous version of the Model Y "that would not have steering wheels or pedals and would be good for transporting groups of 6 or 7 people," according to Benzinga.

The new Model Y would sit alongside the Cybercab, Tesla's two-seat Robotaxi, which Musk has said could handle the majority of passenger miles. "We still need autonomous vehicles if you've got 4 or 6, or a whole family," he said, though he offered no further details or timeline.

Musk made the remarks when asked whether Tesla's business would focus solely on autonomy going forward. His answer pointed to a lineup built around seating needs rather than driving.

"It's going to make sense for us to make cars that can seat different amounts of people," he said.

Elon Musk plans for new Model Y with no steering wheel

Musk also had praise for the Model Y L, the six-seat version of the SUV, calling it Tesla's "most popular" model. "I think we should probably change all the Model Y production to the Y L because it's what most people seem to want," Musk said, according to Benzinga.

Also read: Elon Musk gives SpaceX stock investors something new to consider

The Model Y matters because it carries Tesla's business. Nearly all the vehicles Tesla delivered in the third quarter were Model 3 sedans and Model Y SUVs, with the Cybertruck and other models making up only a sliver of sales.

It already does much of the work in Tesla's driverless fleet as well. Most of the Robotaxis Tesla has registered in Texas are Cybercab vehicles, while a smaller group of modified Model Y is on the road in Austin, with Dallas expected to follow.

Related: How much TSLA stock does Tesla CEO Elon Musk actually own?

Tesla goes all in on the Cybercab

Musk is putting serious money behind the two-seater. Tesla plans to spend about $3.3 billion expanding its factory near Berlin, with a new building designed to produce up to 1 million vehicles a year, Reuters confirmed.

Construction is expected to start in the first half of 2027, and Cybercab production there is planned for 2029.

The Cybertruck is making way at home. On Nov. 5, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory to free up space for the Cybercab, adding that the order backlog is "far more than we can make before dismantling the line," EV reported.

Tesla shares rose about 5% the next day.

The exit will take a little longer than first planned. Musk has since pushed the end of production to late summer 2027 to fill open orders, and buyers who do not get a truck will have their deposits returned.
